Writing renderer plugins

A plugin turns an input (a file, a value, or one element of a list) into one or more output files. Use one when templates aren't enough: rendering text to a motion graphic, generating OpenGraph cards, minifying, syntax highlighting, converting formats.

PLUGIN motion FROM ./plugins/motion.mjs [INTEGRITY sha256:…]
TRANSFORM ./title.txt WITH motion TO /title.svg OPTIONS style=typewriter duration=2
TRANSFORM WITH motion TO /cards/${post.slug}.svg OPTIONS text=${post.title} FOR post IN posts

See examples/motion/ for a complete plugin (text → animated SVG).

The module

A JavaScript plugin is one ES module file ending in .mjs, in its own folder (for example ./plugins/motion.mjs). Export transform, or a default object with it:

export const apiVersion = 1;

export async function transform(request) {
  const text = request.input?.text ?? request.options.text ?? '';
  return { bytes: `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text y="20">${escape(text)}</text></svg>` };
}

The request

{
  apiVersion: 1,
  dest: string,                       // artifact path being written, e.g. "/title.svg"
  options: Record<string, string>,    // OPTIONS key=value … (always strings; ${ARG} and ${item.key} are interpolated)
  input?: {                           // when the TRANSFORM has a file source
    path: string,                     // "./title.txt", "name:/path", "<<EOF" …
    name: string,                     // file name
    bytes: Uint8Array,
    text?: string,                    // set when the bytes are valid UTF-8
  },
  data?: unknown,                     // when the source is a value import (json, yaml, csv, markdown, wbn)
  item?: unknown,                     // the current element, with FOR item IN list
}

Sources work like COPY's: a local path, name: / name:/path for an import, --from=stage /path, or an inline <<EOF body. With FOR … IN … the source is optional.

The result

Return one of:

  • a string or Uint8Array, or { bytes }: one file written to dest
  • { files: { "a.svg": …, "sub/b.png": … } }: several files under dest, which should end in /; keys are relative POSIX paths (no ..)

Throwing an Error fails the build with E_PLUGIN and your message. console.log output appears as build warnings prefixed [plugin name].

Writes follow the usual conflict rules: different content at an existing path fails unless the TRANSFORM has --overwrite.

The sandbox

Each plugin runs in its own Node process started with Node's permission model:

node --permission --allow-fs-read=<the plugin's folder> …

| A plugin can | A plugin cannot | | --- | --- | | read files in its own folder (helpers, fonts, data) | read other files, including your project | | import node: built-ins and files in its folder | write files, spawn processes, use workers or native addons | | use CPU and memory | open network connections | | | see environment variables (it gets an empty environment) |

Each call has a time limit (--plugin-timeout, default 60 s) and results are capped at 64 MiB. Processes are stopped when the build ends.

Trust model. Node describes its permission model as a "seat belt" for trusted code, not a defence against deliberately malicious code. Treat a plugin like any dependency: run plugins you trust, keep them in your repository, and pin them with INTEGRITY (which covers the module file itself; other files in its folder are not hashed). Because a plugin can read its whole folder, Sitefile refuses a plugin placed directly in the build context root.

Determinism

Sitefile builds are reproducible, so plugins should be too: produce the same bytes for the same request. Avoid Date.now(), Math.random() and anything that depends on the machine. (Reading the clock is not blocked; it is just a bad idea.)

WebAssembly plugins

PLUGIN name FROM ./plugins/x.wasm loads a WebAssembly module instead of a JavaScript one. Everything else (TRANSFORM, OPTIONS, FOR, INTEGRITY, caching) works the same. See examples/wasm/ for a plugin written in Rust (plugins/badge-src, built with ./build.sh).

The module imports nothing. That is checked when the build starts, and it's what makes wasm plugins the strongest sandbox Sitefile offers: with no imports a module can't open files, use the network, read the clock or get randomness. It can only compute. So a wasm plugin may live anywhere in the context (it can't read its folder), and its results are always cacheable.

ABI v1

Build for wasm32-unknown-unknown (Rust: a cdylib; C: clang --target=wasm32 -nostdlib -Wl,--no-entry -Wl,--export-all; or hand-written WAT) and export:

| Export | Signature | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | memory | memory | the module's linear memory | | sitefile_alloc | (len: i32) -> i32 | reserve len bytes for the request; return a pointer | | sitefile_transform | (ptr: i32, len: i32) -> i64 | read the request at ptr, return (resultPtr << 32) \| resultLen | | sitefile_api_version | () -> i32 | optional; must return 1 |

The request is UTF-8 JSON: the same object JS plugins receive, with input.bytes base64-encoded. The result is UTF-8 JSON, one of:

{ "text": "<svg …>" }
{ "bytes": "<base64>" }
{ "files": { "a.svg": "<base64>", "sub/b.png": "<base64>" } }
{ "error": "option \"color\" must be #rgb" }

Each call gets a fresh instance, so nothing carries over between calls and the module may simply leak its allocations. Calls run in a worker thread that is terminated after --plugin-timeout; linear memory is capped at 1 GiB and results at 64 MiB. Traps, out-of-range results, invalid JSON and {"error"} all fail the build with E_PLUGIN.

External tools: TOOL and --allow-exec

Plugins cannot run programs. For real media output (video, audio, images) a build can instead call an external program such as ffmpeg, but only through an explicit, command-line allow-list:

TOOL ffmpeg
TRANSFORM --overwrite WITH ffmpeg TO /intro.mp4 OPTIONS size=1280x720 \
  ARGS -hide_banner -loglevel error -f lavfi -i "color=c=black:s={option.size}:d=3:r=30" \
       -c:v mpeg4 -fflags +bitexact -flags:v +bitexact -map_metadata -1 {output}

sitefile build --allow-exec ffmpeg                 # looked up on PATH
sitefile build --allow-exec ffmpeg=/opt/bin/ffmpeg # or an absolute path
  • TOOL name only declares the need. Without --allow-exec name the build stops with E_UNSUPPORTED and the exact flag to add. The program is resolved to an absolute real path when the build starts, and printed.
  • A TRANSFORM that names a tool takes a source file as for plugins (or none), OPTIONS, FOR, and last ARGS …: the argv template. Placeholders: {input} (the source, copied to a file in a per-call temp directory), {output} (required; the single file the tool must write; its extension comes from <dest> so tools can pick a format), and {option.key}. Both file placeholders are relative names (input.txt, output.mp4) because the tool's working directory is that temp directory, so filter syntaxes that treat : or , specially need no escaping. Any other {…} is literal.
  • No shell, ever. The program is started with an argv array (spawn(path, argv, { shell: false })). ;, $(…), backticks, *, | in arguments or option values reach the program as plain text. Values are substituted once and never re-scanned. (An argument that starts with - is still an option to the tool: do not put untrusted ${…} values in option position.)
  • Per call: a fresh temp directory (removed afterwards) holding the input; working directory = that directory; environment = PATH=/usr/bin:/bin only (none of your variables or secrets; the OS may add its own); stdin closed; killed after --plugin-timeout (default 60 s); output larger than 64 MiB (or not a regular file, or missing) is rejected. stdout/stderr are kept to their tail and shown as build warnings ([tool ffmpeg] …, at most 20 lines each); use -hide_banner -loglevel error to keep that quiet. A non-zero exit is E_PLUGIN with the last stderr lines.

Trust model, honestly. Node's --permission sandbox only governs Node code: it cannot confine a native binary. A tool runs with your user's privileges and can read or write anything you can, and the network too. The allow-list (you name each program on the command line, the Sitefile cannot widen it) and the missing shell are the controls, not a sandbox. Allow programs you trust, with arguments you have reviewed; a Sitefile from someone else can still make an allowed program do what its arguments permit. Prefer name=/absolute/path when PATH is not trustworthy.

Determinism. Reproducible builds need reproducible tools. ffmpeg embeds its encoder name, timestamps and metadata by default; use -fflags +bitexact -flags:v +bitexact -map_metadata -1 (the test suite checks this gives identical bytes). Multi-threaded encoders can still differ between versions or CPUs. Caching (below) makes repeated builds stable by reusing the first result.

Caching

TRANSFORM results are cached between builds in $SITEFILE_HOME/cache/transform (default ~/.sitefile/cache/transform): an unchanged TRANSFORM is not run again, and the plugin process is not even started (plugins start lazily, on their first cache miss).

The key is the SHA-256 of a canonical JSON (sorted keys) of:

  • the cache format version;
  • the code: for a plugin, a digest of every file in its folder (it can read them all, so any may matter; folders over 2000 files or 128 MiB are not cached, with a warning); for a tool, its resolved real path, size and mtime, and the interpolated ARGS;
  • the request: dest, options, the input (path, name, content digest), the value-import data, and the FOR item.

Results are stored by content hash (entries/<key>.json pointing at blobs/<sha256>). Every read re-verifies each blob's digest and size, so a corrupt or truncated entry is ignored, removed, and rewritten after the rebuild; a cache that cannot be written never fails the build.

Caching assumes deterministic code. A plugin that depends on the clock, randomness, the network or the machine should opt out by exporting cache:

export const cache = false;         // or: export default { apiVersion: 1, cache: false, transform }

Its results are then never stored or reused (it is started on every build). Anything not in the key is invisible to the cache: a tool that reads files other than {input}, or a different version of a tool installed at the same path with the same size and mtime. Use --no-cache to bypass (no reads, no writes), and sitefile cache info|prune to inspect or clear it. The cache neither reads nor changes Sitefile.lock, so --frozen-lockfile is unaffected.
